appraisal_events.evidence: Cela ne prouve pas que les opinions de Bergotte fussent moins valables que celles de l'Ambassadeur, au contraire... Les arguments de M. de Norpois (en matière d'art) étaient sans réplique parce qu'ils étaient sans réalité.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly argues that Bergotte's ideas carry real generative force even when contradicted, whereas Norpois's arguments go unanswered only because they are empty, lowering Norpois's rhetorical standing relative to Bergotte.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mais c'est un vieux serin... il vous a donné des coups de bec parce qu'il croit toujours avoir devant lui un échaudé ou une seiche; Mme Swann: il est ennuyeux comme la pluie... je l'ai trouvé d'un vaseux; closing: il est au contraire très mauvaise langue.
appraisal_events.explanation: Bergotte and Mme Swann jointly mock Norpois as tedious and secretly malicious; Swann's brief, self-consciously adopted defense ('l'emploi d'homme de bon sens') collapses when he himself concedes Norpois is not very interesting, so the household's dismissive judgment stands largely unchallenged.

status_effects.explanation: Norpois's arguments are explicitly characterized as without substance, weakening his intellectual authority relative to Bergotte.
Mocked as tedious and two-faced by Bergotte and Mme Swann, with only a token, quickly abandoned defense from Swann.
The narrator affirms that Bergotte's ideas retain real force even in disagreement, in explicit contrast to Norpois's hollow authority.

ambiguities: The mockery of Norpois (E2) is voiced jointly by Bergotte and Mme Swann; Bergotte is recorded as the primary source but Mme Swann's remarks contribute equally to the diminishment.

Swann's response to the mockery is mixed: he offers a mild defense of Norpois framed ironically by the narrator as an adopted pose ('l'emploi d'homme de bon sens'), then immediately undercuts it by conceding Norpois isn't interesting, so his stance does not materially counterbalance the diminishment.
